ce:caption.ce:simple-para: RNA m6A modification in the SARS-CoV-2 genome. The genome of SARS-CoV-2 exhibits m6A modifications, predominantly located in the ORF1ab region and the 3′ end of the viral RNA. The viral life cycle encompasses several crucial stages: the release of genetic material, translation of viral proteins mediated by eIF4E, replication of the viral RNA genome driven by RdRp, and assembly of new viral particles. Throughout its lifecycle, the level of m6A undergoes dynamic changes. The regulatory role of m6A/hnRNAP1 facilitates the switch of the virus from protein translation to RNA transcription. Significant differences in m6A modifications are observed among different lineages of the SARS-CoV-2, which may be associated with the viral pathogenicity.

Role of m6A modification in virus-host interactions. SARS-CoV-2 enters host cells through either the ACE2 or the transmembrane protein 106B (TMEM106B). In the first scenario (indicated as ①), the virus enters host cells through endocytosis when the cell surface protease TMPRSS2 is insufficient. Alternatively, in the second scenario (indicated as ②), the virus fuses with the cell membrane when the cell surface TMPRSS2 is activated, gaining entry into host cells. Following the invasion of host cells by SARS-CoV-2, there is an increase in the m6A modification level of host RNA, which in turn affects cell death, apoptosis, and metabolic processes in the host. Additionally, the virus alters the distribution of METTL3 within the nucleus and cytoplasm and enhances the expression of pro-viral genes mediated by METTL3, such as ACE2, TMPRSS2, and CTSL. After m6A modification of the viral genome by METTL3, the binding of viral RNA to RIG-I is inhibited, thereby blocking the activation of NF-κB and IRF3 pathways and reducing the production of inflammatory cytokines and interferons. Furthermore, the interaction between the viral polymerase RdRp and METTL3 suppresses the sumoylation and ubiquitination processes of METTL3.

Potential Applications of m6A Modification in COVID-19 Patients. In patients with COVID-19, a significant increase in the level of m6A modification has been observed in lung tissues and blood samples. To date, three types of predictive models and pharmacological interventions have been developed. Some of these drugs have already been validated at the cellular level (indicated in bold).
Summary of the studies on RNA m6A modification of SARS-CoV-2 genome.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Since December 2019, the infection caused by Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus Type 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has posed an enormous threat to human health security worldwide. Constant mutation of viral genome and varying therapeutic responses of patients infected with this virus prompted efforts to uncover more novel regulators in the pathogenesis. The involvement of N6-methyladenosine, a modified form of RNA, plays a crucial role in viral replication, viral pathogenicity, and intricate signaling pathways connected with immune responses. This review discusses research advances revealing the regulation of the life cycle of SARS-CoV-2 and antiviral responses of host cells by RNA m6A modification, highlights the biological functions of N6-methyladenosine components in SARS-CoV-2 infection and virus-host interactions, and outlines current challenges and future directions for exploring the potential clinical value of m6A modification in COVID-19.

ce:list-item.ce:para: RNA m6A modification in SARS-CoV-2 genome significantly affects viral replication and pathogenicity.
RNA m6A modification in host cell genome can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection, altering antiviral responses of host cells to SARS-CoV-2 through a variety of mechanisms.
RNA m6A modification and m6A enzymes serve as promising prognostic factors and therapeutic targets for COVID-19.

ce:keyword.ce:text: Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus Type 2 (SARS-CoV-2)

ce:section.ce:para: Corona Virus Disease 2019 (COVID-19), which is caused by the infection with Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus Type 2 (SARS-CoV-2), has remained a global public health threat since December 2019. As of June 2023, the pandemic has resulted in over 771 million individuals being infected, leading to a distressing loss of life nearly 7 million people (https://covid19.who.int/data). Although a great deal of money and resources have been spent on vaccine research, the existing vaccines does not completely protect against the novel coronavirus as the virus continues to mutate. Till today, SARS-CoV-2 infection keeps attacking many countries and regions, and causing a great number of deaths, even though vaccination and antiviral agents against SARS-CoV-2 are popularized. Therefore, novel effective prevention and treatment of SARS-CoV-2 infection are urgently required.

N6-methyladenosine (m6A) represents a form of RNA modification with crucial biological roles in the viral life cycle and the modulation of host cell antiviral responses. Notably, the presence of m6A modification in SARS-CoV-2 has been unveiled. This review discusses the evolving significance of m6A modification in regulating SARS-CoV-2 pathogenicity and virus-host interactions, with a specific emphasis on its potential impact on the severity and prognosis of COVID-19.

ce:section.ce:section-title: RNA m6A modification in mammalian and viruses
ce:section.ce:para: Epigenetic transcriptomics (also known as "RNA epigenetics") refers to RNA post-transcriptional modifications. These modifications are involved in regulating various aspects of RNA metabolism, thus affecting gene expression and multiple biological processes. The association between RNA modifications and a variety of human diseases has been scientifically verified, including but not limited to various types of cancers [1,2], nerve damage [3], metabolic diseases, etc.

The m6A modification is a result of methylation occurring at the sixth nitrogen atom (N) of adenine. This specific alteration was first documented in 1974 and is widely observed in mRNA of eukaryotes, composing more than 80% of all methylation modifications found in RNA [4]. In 2012, Dominissini and Meyer developed a novel technique to map the whole m6A to a large number of mammalian transcriptomes, and they found that regions exhibiting elevated levels of m6A are located in close proximity to the termination codon and within the 3′ untranslated regions (3′ UTRs) [5,6]. At the same time, other researchers identified that m6A is mainly present in DRACH motif and GGACU motif [7]. In the 1970s, influenza A virus and adenovirus were found to have m6A modification sites [8,9]. During the past years, the involvement of m6A in viral life cycle and its impact on antiviral responses have been verified. The regulation of m6A modification on the life cycle of various viruses can be different, or even opposite. The knockdown of methyltransferase-like protein (METTL3) and methyltransferase-like protein 14 (METTL14) increases the production of Endogenous retroviruses [10] and Zika virus [11], but it inhibits the replication of human respiratory syncytial virus [12]. Similarly, m6A modification can upregulate the expression of human immunodeficiency virus 1 in HEK293T cells, while negatively affecting its expression in CD4 + T lymphocytes [13,14].

Recently, the presence of m6A modification has been confirmed in the SARS-CoV-2 genome. m6A modification is regulated by various m6A enzymes within host cells [15]. Specifically, the m6A modification has been found to be associated with the clinical conditions of COVID-19 patients [16]. This connection has prompted researchers to focus closely on its potential role as a promising and innovative therapeutic target for COVID-19.
The dynamic balance of m6A modification in RNA is regulated by the methylation modification of "writers", the demethylation of "erasers", and the recognition of "readers".

The writers of m6A refer to multiple methyltransferases that work as complexes. METTL3 and METTL14 are the first stable heteronuclear dimers found in methyltransferase complexes [17]. METTL3 acts as S-adenosine binding protein, which has the capacity of methyltransferase, and METTL14 can promote the binding of RNA and complex. They collaborate to play a crucial role in RNA m6A modification. Subsequently, Wilms Tumor 1 associated protein (WTAP) binds METTL3 to METTL14, and induces METTL3-METTL14 complex localization, thereby promoting complex activity [18]. RNA binding motif protein 15/15B (RBM15/15B) acts as part of the complexes that promote the binding to specific RNA sites [19]. Besides, VIRMA (KIAA1429), ZC3H13, CBLL1 (HAKAI), and METTL16 [20–23] have also been observed to interact with components of methyltransferase complex.

Erasers of m6A can remove methyl groups from RNA, resulting in a modification of the m6A surface that undergoes dynamic and reversible changes. Eraser mainly includes obesity-associated protein (FTO) and AlkB homolog 5 (ALKHB5) [24,25]. FTO has been recognized as the first m6A eraser that is connected with obesity and can regulate cellular energy homeostasis [24]. The identification of ALKBH5 confirms the existence of another demethylase responsible for m6A modification [25]. FTO and ALKBH5 exhibit distinct expression patterns across various tissues and cell types.

The m6A readers refer to the proteins that demonstrate specific affinity for RNA and are involved in regulating the processing, translation, and degradation of RNA sequences containing m6A modifications. Readers can be categorized into three distinct groups: readers containing YTH domain, hnRNP family and readers containing the same RNA binding domain. Readers containing YTH domain mainly including YTHDF1–3 and YTHDC1–2 [26–28]. These readers exert different regulatory effects in regulating RNA translation, degradation, splicing and translocation [29]. Besides, hnRNP family contains hnRNPC, hnRNPG and hnRNPA2B1, and readers containing the same RNA binding domain include FMR1 and IGF2BP1–3 [30].

Currently, there are many applicable methods to detect RNA m6A modification. In 2012, a novel high-throughput technology named as m6A-methylated RNA immunoprecipitation (MeRIP) was developed to measure m6A levels in both humans and mice 5,6. Additionally, liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and colorimetric m6A RNA methylation assay offer alternative ways to obtain the overall m6A methylation level on RNA. In order to study the specific RNA region with m6A methylation modification, MeRIP-sequencing is utilized based on the principle of m6A specific antibody recognition and binding to m6A sites on mRNA, RNA immunoprecipitation method to enrich m6A-modified fragments, and integrates with RNA sequencing technology [5]. Although MeRIP-sequencing allows the identification of m6A hypermethylation regions, it cannot achieve single-base resolution. Subsequently, m6A individual-nucleotide-resolution cross-linking and immunoprecipitation sequencing (miCLIP-seq) detects single-base methylation levels by cross-linking the RNA-m6A antibody binding sites. Direct RNA sequencing (DRS) based on nanopore technology is a technology that directly measure natural RNA without reverse transcription. It can obtain base modification information while reading the RNA base sequence [31]. Moreover, due to the significance of m6A modification in SARS-CoV-2 infection, accessible software packages have been developed and can be used to predict m6A modification sites in viral genome based on sequence features, such as SRAMP and RFAthM6A [32,33]. Recently, Liu and colleagues created a machine-learning model to accurately predict m6A modification sites in SARS-CoV-2 genome via using DRS raw data [34].

As a member of the Coronaviridae family, SARS-CoV-2 is an enveloped virus featuring a positive single-stranded RNA genome, which is approximately 30 kilobases long. After infecting host cells, SARS-CoV-2 uses its own genomic RNA as a template for replication and translation in cytoplasm [35]. It encodes proteins that can be divided into three major categories, namely structural proteins, nonstructural proteins, and accessory proteins [36]. The mature SARS-CoV-2 virus is composed of viral genome and structural proteins, while non-structural proteins and accessory proteins exert the functions that facilitate viral replication and combat the host immune response to virus infection.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Dynamic changes of m6A modification in SARS-CoV-2 genome
ce:section.ce:para: Abundant literatures show that RNA m6A modification is widely distributed in SARS-CoV-2 genome. Li and colleagues purified SARS-CoV-2 from Vero E6 cells and detected a series of m6A modification sites in viral RNA using LC-MS/MS [37]. They discovered that m6A modification constituted approximately 0.096% of the adenosine residues in the viral RNA, with an estimated eight m6A modification sites identified within the virus. These m6A peaks were notably located in the 3′ end of ORF1ab and the genomic RNA, with a specific concentration in the N region. In another research, Liu et al. simultaneously used MeRIP-seq and miCLIP to analyze the SARS-CoV-2 genome, and they observed eight overlapping m6A peaks identified in the two tests [38]. Three m6A peaks were found in ORF1ab, three in the N region, one in ORF 7a, and one in ORF 10. Among them, five m6A peaks have been verified in SARS-CoV-2 RNA by other researchers, which are located at ORF1ab, N region and ORF10 39. Burgess et al. also reported 14 stable and reproducible peaks on SARS-CoV-2 genome, which overlapped with the m6A peaks reported in previous studies [40]. These findings confirm the presence of m6A modification in the SARS-CoV-2 genome, mainly distributed in ORF1ab and the 3′ end of viral RNA.

RNA m6A modification undergoes dynamic and reversible changes during the pathogenesis of SARS-CoV-2 infection. Liu and colleagues observed four m6A peaks on SARS-CoV-2 RNA at 24 h post-infection and an additional nine m6A peaks at 56 h post-infection [38]. In Vero E6 cells, measurements of SARS-CoV-2 RNA m6A levels at various time points (1, 2, 4, and 6 h post-infection) revealed a significant elevation in m6A levels at 2 h post-infection compared to the levels at other time points [41]. Therefore, dynamic methylation controlled by m6A regulators during host cell infection could explain the observed variations in m6A levels and the number of m6A peaks across different experimental analyses conducted on the SARS-CoV-2 genome.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Influences of RNA m6A modification on SARS-CoV-2 replication and pathogenicity
ce:section.ce:para: RNA m6A modification and m6A enzymes exert significant functions in SRAS-COV-2 infection. In a recent study, diverse m6A modification sites were observed in the genomic RNA of various SARS-CoV-2 lineages, encompassing Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, Lambda, and Omicron, each exhibiting distinct pathogenicity. Significantly, researchers found a correlation between the number of m6A modification sites in the N region and specific m6A sites with the severity of COVID-19 [42]. Notably, substantial variations in global m6A levels were identified in nasopharyngeal samples from Mexican patients infected with different SARS-CoV-2 variants. This consistent evidence supports the association of RNA m6A modification with SARS-CoV-2 pathogenicity, displaying variability across viral lineages [43].

Pharmacological inhibition or knockdown of m6A enzymes in host cells affects the replication and pathogenicity of SARS-CoV-2. Selective inhibition of FTO by rhein causes a prominent decrease of SARS-CoV-2 infectivity [44]. The administration of DZNep, a methyltransferase inhibitor, reduced the m6A level on SARS-CoV-2 RNA, leading to the decrease of RNA replication in Vero cells. Subsequently, decreased synthesis of 5′ cap of viral mRNA impeding its interaction with eIF4E, a key regulator of mRNA translation, thus inhibiting viral protein synthesis [41]. In Caco-2 cells, Li et al. observed that the m6A level in N region of the viral genome decreased after knocking down METTL3 by small hairpin RNA, and the viral load also decreased after the knockdown of METTL3 or METTL14 [37]. Consistently, another study showed that knocking out METTL3 significantly reduced SARS-CoV-2 viral titer and N protein expression in Vero cells; on the contrary, knocking out FTO increased the viral titer [39]. Burgess et al. reported that m6A enzymes affected SARS-CoV-2 amplification through regulating viral RNA replication and nucleocapsid synthesis. Silence of METTL3 by small interfering RNA reduced the proportion of SARS-CoV-2-infected host cells by approximately 80%; meanwhile, silencing YTHDF2 and YTHDF3 led to the decrease of infected cells by 42%− 66% and 75%− 76%, respectively [40]. Researchers further reported that METTL3 interacted with SARS-CoV-2 RNA in Vero E6 cells using formalin-crosslinked RNA immunoprecipitation, which increased the expression of the SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp); elevated level of RdRp upregulated the expression of METTL3, and vice versa 39. Based on the knowledge that RdRp is responsible for viral RNA replication, METTL3 could be a crucial regulator that affect viral replication and titers through SARS-CoV-2 RdRp. However, another study showed that knockdown of METTL3, METTL14 or YTHDF2 markedly promoted viral replication and increased the presence of SARS-CoV-2-infected cells, in contrast to knockdown of ALKBH5, which reduced viral replication [38]. These intriguing findings illustrate that various elements of the m6A modification system collaborate intricately to perform diverse functions in the pathogenesis of COVID-19.

A series of research data on RNA m6A modification of SARS-CoV-2 genome are summarized in Table 1. As shown in Fig. 1, these studies support that m6A enzymes are significantly involved in regulating SARS-CoV-2 replication and infection capacity through a variety of mechanisms. Recently, an updated database named as RMDisease V2.0 and containing numerous genetic variants that affect m6A modification of SARS-CoV-2 genomic RNA has been developed [45]. By utilizing this database, researchers have easy access to further explore the correlation between COVID-19 and m6A modification-associated variants.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Regulation of virus-host interactions by RNA m6A modification
ce:section.ce:para: The connection between RNA m6A modification and virus-host interactions has garnered growing support from numerous studies. Upon the binding of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein to angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) or transmembrane protein 106B (TMEM106B) in human airway epithelial cells, it initiates host immune responses, consequently leading to pathophysiological changes [46]. A crucial initial stage in the host innate immune response to SARS-CoV-2 infection involves the production of type I and type III interferons (IFN-I and IFN-III, respectively), along with the production of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines [47]. The adaptive immune response encompasses CD4 + T cells, CD8 + T cells, and specific antibodies. Studies indicate a more prominent response of CD4 + T cells to SARS-CoV-2, particularly in the rapid clearance of the virus during acute infection [48]. In contrast, the presence of CD8 + T cells is correlated with a favorable prognosis in COVID-19 [49]. Following infection, the majority of COVID-19 patients rapidly generate neutralizing antibodies that confer protective effects against SARS-CoV-2, offering valuable insights for vaccine development [50].

It is well acknowledged that m6A modification and its downstream signaling pathways are heavily involved in modulation of immune responses, such as the activation and infiltration of immune cells and the production of interferon-γ [51]. The epitranscriptomic m6A profile of human lung cells undergoes significant changes following infection with SARS-CoV-2, and these changes may have a profound impact on the host cell's RNA [52]. The abundance of methylation sites in host cell RNA also undergoes alterations upon SARS-CoV-2 infection, potentially leading to increased RNA instability [53]. This instability in host RNA could have implications for the host's innate immunity response to the virus.

The m6A modification plays a crucial role in regulating interactions between SARS-CoV-2 and host cells. Specifically, it targets the interferon-mediated immune response and various other pathways [54]. The detailed understanding of these regulatory mechanisms is essential for unraveling the complexities of the host-virus interaction and may provide valuable insights for developing targeted therapeutic interventions against SARS-CoV-2. In METTL3-depleted Caco-2 cells, gene expression levels of ACE2, TMPRSS2 (encoding Transmembrane Serine Protease) and CTSL (encoding Cathepsin L), which are required for facilitating SARS-CoV-2 entry into host cells, were significantly downregulated [37]. This could contribute to the decreased viral load caused by METTL3 depletion after SARS-CoV-2 infection. The study by Meng et al. demonstrated that the m6A level in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) of COVID-19 patients is significantly higher than in healthy controls. The subsequent m6A epitranscriptomic microarray revealed that aberrant methylation triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection regulates multiple target genes associated with immune response and cell death pathways in PBMCs [55]. Similarly, in BEAS-2B cells after SARS-CoV-2 infection, m6A modification was reported to regulate various pathways, including type I interferon signaling, cilium organization and assembly, etc [56]. Notably, Li et al. discovered that increased m6A modification in SARS-CoV-2 RNA hinders its binding to retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I), a crucial pattern recognition receptor. This inhibition leads to enhanced phosphorylation of IRF3 and IκBα, consequently impeding the host's immune responses against virus infection. This includes the suppression of type I interferon signaling and the production of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines [37]. In SARS-CoV-2-infected Huh7 cells, METTL14 and ALKBH5 were translocated into the cytoplasm from the nucleus, increasing m6A levels in the coding sequence region and decreasing m6A levels in the 3′ UTR region. This led to alterations in interferon-stimulated genes, membrane trafficking, and apoptosis signaling in host cells [38]. In human lung A549 epithelial cells, SARS-CoV-2 infection induced distinct m6A modifications in various mRNA and noncoding RNA species, associated with pathways related to protein processing in the endoplasmic reticulum, cell apoptosis, and proliferation [52]. These differentially methylated mRNAs were regulated by upstream regulators involved in the cellular response to type I interferon, inflammatory response, and cytokine signaling. Furthermore, m6A modification has also been observed in transcripts involved in mRNA translation into protein, peptide and amine metabolism following SARS-CoV-2 infection in both Vero cells and Calu-3 cells [57].

Type I interferon signaling regulated by m6A modification has also been observed in other viral infections. According to a recent study, m6A modification facilitated by METTL3 is required for enhancing mRNA stability and increasing protein translation of host cells, which consequently ensures the efficacy of antiviral immunity. Furthermore, METTL3 deficiency leads to severely impaired induction of type I interferon signaling, a crucial signal pathway for antiviral immune responses and combating viral infections, in influenza virus-infected macrophages and mice [58]. In patients with condyloma acuminata, WTAP is found to be a key regulator for upregulating the expression of IFN-ε (an important component of type I interferon signaling) by promoting its m6A modification, and consequently enhance antiviral response to HPV infection [59]. Based on the knowledge that type I interferon plays a critical protective role against SARS-CoV-2 infection [60], these findings strongly support the notion that the type I interferon signaling pathway is a crucial link through which m6A modification affects SARS-CoV-2 infection.

How the m6A modification regulates host cell responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection is depicted in Fig. 2. Detailed research data on RNA m6A modification of host cell genome following SARS-CoV-2 infection are listed in Table 2. Overall, findings in recent studies suggest that m6A modification regulates virus-host interaction through variable mechanisms, mainly through immune signaling pathways. It is difficult to conclude whether alterations in host immune responses caused by m6A modification are beneficial to COVID-19 patients or not. In most cases, the production of cytokines and chemokines controls viral replication and enhance the host defense. However, the formation of cytokine storm, referring to an uncontrolled over-production of proinflammatory mediators, will lead to a poor prognosis of COVID-19.

ce:section.ce:section-title: The m6A modification as a Therapeutic Target and Predictive Factor for COVID-19
Pharmacological interventions in the m6A modification
ce:section.ce:para: The m6A modification has emerged as a potential therapeutic target for COVID-19. In vitro, Burgess et al. reported that METTL3 inhibitor STM2457 reduced the percentage of virus-infected cells, and the effect was enhanced with increasing doses and was not caused by the toxicity of STM2457 itself [40]. In previous studies, the primary focus of research on STM2457 has been directed towards inhibiting cancer growth. There have been reports indicating promising applications of STM2457 in various cancers such as acute myeloid leukemia, small cell lung cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, osteosarcoma, among others [61–64]. Additionally, researchers conducted in vivo experiments using mice and found that STM2457 can effectively target leukemia cells without compromising the functionality of normal hematopoietic stem cells and other normal cells, demonstrating a high level of safety [61]. DZNep, an S-adenosylmethionine dependent methyltransferase inhibitor, has shown promise in reducing SARS-CoV-2 replication and protein synthesis in a dose-dependent manner [41]. In previous studies, DZNep has been explored for its potential in combating tumors by inhibiting the histone methyltransferase (EZH2). However, DZNeP, characterized by hydrophilicity and rapid renal metabolism, has limited clinical utility [65]. Additionally, a series of FTO inhibitors have been synthetized and display anticancer effects in vitro, but most of them are still at the stage of preclinical study. Repressing the catalytic function of FTO by rhein leads to a significant reduction in the infectivity of different coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2, without causing any rise in cytotoxicity within Vero cells [44]. However, FTO inhibitors such as rhein, meclofenamate sodium, and MO-I-500 face limitations in their clinical prospects due to their mild functionality, low sensitivity and specificity [66]. Current research on small molecules such as methyltransferase inhibitors and FTO inhibitors is largely confined to in vitro experiments and animal studies. Further investigation is needed to assess the potential toxicity of these small molecules in human applications. Ensuring specificity to viral RNA without adversely affecting essential cellular processes is a critical challenge. As of now, there are no approved pharmaceuticals or compounds specifically designed to inhibit or activate m6A enzymes for administration in the human body. Clinical application of m6A-targeting interventions is still in its early stages. The transition from preclinical studies to human trials requires thorough validation of safety, efficacy, and specificity. With the growing knowledge of m6A's involvement in COVID-19, there is a hopeful prospect for the development of therapeutic agents specifically targeting m6A.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Correlation between the m6A modification and COVID-19 severity/prognosis
ce:section.ce:para: Currently, the correlation between m6A modification and COVID-19 severity and prognosis is an area of active research. Analysis on blood samples of hospitalized COVID-19 patients showed a higher level of m6A modification than non-COVID-19 ones [67]. Li et al. conducted an analysis of lung samples from deceased COVID-19 patients and healthy lung biopsy samples to explore gene expression patterns associated with the disease. The study noted increased expression levels of inflammatory genes and interferon-stimulated genes in COVID-19 patients, and there was a significant decrease in the expression of METTL3 and METTL14 genes [37]. Lu et al. utilized RNA-sequencing data from blood samples, comparing healthy controls with COVID-19 patients. Noteworthy differences in gene expression levels were identified among 11 m6A regulators, including WTAP, RBM15 /15B, YTHDC1, etc. But no difference was observed in METTL3 and METTL14 genes. Subsequently, the researchers developed a nomogram model using seven m6A regulators to predict the risk of COVID-19, which could facilitate the identification of individuals with high risk and enables early intervention [68]. Additionally, expression levels of IFN-stimulated genes and IL-8 in the alveolar epithelium of severe COVID-19 patients were significantly higher and METTL3 expression was significantly lower than healthy controls and moderate COVID-19 patients. Compared with healthy controls, there were 1953 mRNAs showing significant hypermethylation and 1191 mRNAs showing significant hypomethylation in COVID-19 patients, and more methylation was upregulated in severe COVID-19 [55]. The variations in observations regarding m6A modification and COVID-19 could stem from several factors, including dynamic changes of m6A modification, differences in sample sources, and insufficient sample size etc. There may be variations and challenges in the current observations, but it is clear that m6A modification plays a role in the development of COVID-19. Further research, especially in larger and more diverse populations, is essential to clarify the specific mechanisms and correlations between m6A modification and COVID-19 severity, as well as its potential as a therapeutic target or diagnostic tool.

Besides, based on differentially expressed genes data between COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 patients, Qiu and colleagues developed an outcome prediction model using nine selected genes associated with m6A modification; the calculated m6A signature score was significantly correlated with important clinical indicators, such as SOFA score, APACHE-II score and ventilator-free days [69]. The findings reported by Qing et al., highlighting a significantly higher level of m6A modification in COVID-19 patients compared to non-COVID-19 patients using transcriptional data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database, present an intriguing aspect of m6A modification in the context of the disease [67]. The m6A subtypes are used to distinguish COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 cases, which offers a novel approach for evaluating the severity and prognosis of COVID-19. These models introduce innovative methods to predict the severity and outcomes of SARS-CoV-2 infection by measuring m6A modification-related factors. In a summary, the role of m6A modification as a potential therapeutic target and predictive factor for COVID-19 is shown in Fig. 3.

In summary, m6A modification demonstrates a multifaceted involvement in COVID-19 pathogenesis. Extensive research underscores its pivotal role in regulating viral replication and the host immune response to the infection. Moreover, the correlation between m6A levels and the severity and prognosis of COVID-19 is becoming increasingly apparent. Identifying comprehensive m6A modification signatures in SARS-CoV-2 could significantly aid in novel vaccine development. Targeting the reduction of virus replication and infection capability through specific small molecule inhibitors offers a promising avenue in antiviral therapy. While investigations into therapeutic drugs targeting m6A are still in their nascent stages, the ongoing dedication to designing and refining m6A-based approaches as potential alternative vaccines and therapies for COVID-19 holds substantial clinical significance.
